interactions.summary: Several students rank Jiang's three lust examples differently, debating whether the greatest sin is exploiting another person, retreating into fantasy, or severing love from a real human relation altogether.

Jiang resolves the exercise by calling the AI-wife case the default worst sin because it signals despair and self-abandonment, while also granting that coercive prostitution would become worse once direct harm to another person is introduced.

speaker_notes.note: These are substantive student replies to Jiang's ranking exercise rather than standalone public questions.
The student objection presses Jiang's own rule that sins harming others are worse, and Jiang narrows the scenario to keep the thought experiment about despair rather than coercion.

claims.claim: One student argues that paying a prostitute is worst because it directly damages another person's future capacity to love, while the other two examples primarily damage the self.

Another student argues that an AI wife is worst because it is not a real person and therefore cannot sustain real love, while the other two examples still preserve some possibility of human relationship.
A student maps the examples onto a triangle of love and says the prostitute and celebrity cases each preserve one aspect of love, while the robot case preserves none.
Jiang's own answer is that the AI-wife case is usually worst because it expresses despair and the abandonment of self-seriousness.
For Dante and the Catholic framework Jiang is using, the worst lust is not raw bodily indulgence but giving up on yourself and settling for a substitute companionship.
Jiang treats coercion as a separate aggravating condition: if paying for sex coerces the other person, then that case becomes much worse because it now harms another person's life directly.

signature_moments.moment: The AI wife becomes the emblem of lust as despair rather than appetite.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you've basically given up on yourself
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens Jiang's whole reinterpretation of lust as surrender of personhood rather than excess desire.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang defines the robotic marriage as a confession that one no longer takes oneself seriously.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you don't take yourself seriously anymore
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This ties the modern thought experiment back to faith, hope, and love as a standard of human dignity.

signature_moments.moment: The student forces a conditional distinction between self-abandonment and directly corrupting another person's life.
signature_moments.source_phrase: sins that impact others are worse
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps the lecture's ranking system honest and previews Jiang's later descent into violence and coercion.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's reading of the worst lust as giving up on oneself and accepting an unreal substitute for love.
The stance Jiang says faith, hope, and love require: treating one's life as worthy of real action and real relation.

chronology_notes.note: This packet shows Jiang testing his Dante model live against contemporary examples and student objections rather than delivering it only as lecture monologue.

uncertainty_notes.note: The ASR is noisy in the student's theological explanation, but the argumentative gist is clear: a human marriage can still open onto God and reproduction in a way a robot relation cannot.
